Walter Hines Page
U.S. Ambassador · Court of St. James's

He named it Garran Hill.
He never spent a night here.

Bought 1,000 acres in February 1913. The ambassadorship came six weeks later. He sailed for London in May. He directed construction from 3,000 miles away, writing to his son Ralph: "The farm — the farm — the farm."

1855 – 1918

Ambassador.
Publisher.
Farmer — in theory.

He co-founded Doubleday Page & Co. He edited the Atlantic Monthly. Appointed by Wilson. He was the most consequential American voice in Britain during the First World War.

He returned to Pinehurst in December 1918. His last words, at Aberdeen station: "Well, Frank, I did get here after all, didn't I?" He died that evening.

Westminster Abbey: "The friend of Britain in her sorest need."

Leonard Tufts provided the craftsmen — the same men building Pinehurst two miles away.

The Threshold

The door has been open since 1916.

GARRAN HILL · 1916 — inlaid in the threshold brick before ground was ever broken.
The hardware was specified in 1916. It has not been replaced.
That is not maintenance. That is devotion.

The Entry Hall

The staircase has turned the same curve since 1916.

Herringbone brick. Leaded glass sidelights. Arched fanlights. The mahogany volute — original. The brass key plates on every door still have their original keys.

The Rooms
The Drawing Room

Fire going,
no one home yet.

Georgian carved mantel. Delft tile surround — blue and white, hand-painted, original. The coffered ceiling was enlarged for dancing.

The Salon

Nearly forty feet long.
Tall windows on both sides.

One end anchored by a fireplace. The proportions have not changed since 1916.

The Dining Room

The shell cabinets were already there in 1916.
They are still there now.

Original 1916 frontispiece. Shell cabinets built in. The proportions — 17 by 19 feet — unchanged. The room draws the same light it always has.

The Library

The room the man who founded Doubleday would have claimed.

Dead center of the first floor. Three walls of shelving, floor to ceiling. Rolling ladder. French doors. Designed 2000.

The Kitchen

White cabinetry.
Dark granite. Island.
Wall of windows.

The kitchen is not original to 1916. It is original to the restoration. Reclaimed heart-pine floors. Two farm sinks. Butler's pantry. The windows face elder magnolias and American plane trees.

The Staircase

Mahogany volute. Original 1916. The same curve, the same wood, the same light.

The Primary Suite

Designed from scratch in 2000
to match 1916 proportions.

Every panel, every cabinet, the fireplace surround — drawn from scratch. Fifteen architectural sheets survive. You cannot tell the difference. That was the point.

The Powder Room

Fuchsia chinoiserie wallpaper. Tennessee marble vanity. Every room needs a laugh.

The Grounds
4.15 Acres

The world outside these gates
does not exist here.

The house sits inside the circle. The trees were saplings in 1916. Every one was planted by hand.

The Pool

20 × 40.
Saltwater. Brick surround.
Wrought iron arch gate.

You cannot see the pool from the road. The rose garden is adjacent. The brick is original. The iron arch is original.

Betty Dumaine · 1959 – 1984
Betty Dumaine · Garran Hill · 1959 – 1984

Betty Dumaine kept the hounds running
and the house alive.

Fox hounds. Peacocks. Horses. One Irish Hunter named Blue Fox — buried at the back of the property, brass marker, slate cover.

Someone still puts flowers there.

The Restoration
Restored 1999 – 2001

The restoration did not make Garran Hill new.
It made the house legible again.

Seven carved mantels saved. Original oak floors lifted, repaired, relaid. Matching the old brick took three months. Custom Marvin windows. Original leaded glass sidelights preserved. The brass hardware — original keys still present on every door.

Full brick. Formal proportion. Restored with the discipline of the original house.

The O'Shea Drawings
15 Architectural Drawings · Thomas O'Shea · 2000

Fifteen O'Shea drawings.
The house drawn before it was restored.
They transfer with the property.

Every panel, every mantel, every window — drawn, specified, approved. The restoration was not improvised. It was documented.
